sec.title: Background
sec.p: The current standard of care for resectable locally advanced colon cancer (LACC) is based on upfront surgery followed by adjuvant chemotherapy (AC). This study aimed to evaluate the safety and efficacy of neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC) in this setting.

sec.title: Patients and methods
sec.p: ELECLA is a multicenter, randomized, open-label, phase II controlled trial conducted across 12 hospitals in Spain between March 2017 and June 2024. This report presents the results of a preplanned interim analysis conducted after early termination of recruitment following the loss of clinical equipoise. Patients with radiologically defined LACC (T3 > 5 mm/T4, any N, and M0) and proficient mismatch repair status, were randomly assigned at a 1:1 ratio to receive either NAC (three cycles of CAPOX or five of FOLFOX), surgery, and AC (investigational group) or upfront surgery followed by AC (control group). The primary endpoint was 2-year disease-free survival.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: A total of 120 patients were included. The NAC completion rate was 94.2%, with a nonsignificant trend toward a reduced surgical complication rate compared with controls (17.3% versus 22.1%; P = 0.52). In the investigational group, a favorable radiologic tumor downstaging was achieved, with a tumor volume reduction of 65.4% (P < 0.001), and a tumor regression grading of 0-2 in 51.2% of assessable patients. An R0 resection was achieved in all patients within the NAC group. A relevant reduction in classical histological adverse prognostic features, including lymphatic invasion (21.5% versus 44.1%; P = 0.009), tumor budding (23.3% versus 58.5%; P = 0.002), and incomplete resections (0% versus 7.4%; P = 0.068) was observed in the NAC group. The 2-year disease-free survival rate was 88.9% [95% confidence interval (CI) 75.2% to 95.2%] in the intervention group and 83.3% (95% CI 70.9% to 90.7%) in the control group (P = 0.34).

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: NAC is safe, feasible, and associated with improved tumor downstaging and favorable pathologic features without increased perioperative morbidity. These findings support the use of NAC as a safe and efficient therapeutic option in patients with LACC.
Key words: colon cancer, neoadjuvant chemotherapy, treatment response

list-item.p: A short course of fluoropyrimidine–oxaliplatin chemotherapy was well tolerated and enabled oncologically adequate surgery.
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy did not significantly improve survival but was associated with better local control and radiologic and pathologic downstaging.
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy was not associated with an increased risk of postoperative surgical complications.
Accurate preoperative staging remains a key challenge for broader implementation of neoadjuvant strategies.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Colorectal cancer remains a major public health concern due to its high incidence.1,2 Recently, the management of rectal cancer has undergone a paradigm shift with the introduction of total neoadjuvant therapy and nonoperative strategies in selected patients.3 However, the implementation of neoadjuvant strategies in resectable locally advanced colon cancer (LACC) has progressed more slowly.4 LACC is defined as a tumor with transmural invasion exceeding 5 mm beyond the colonic wall or with radiologically suspected nodal involvement (T3>5 mm-4N0M0 or T1-4N+M0). Oncologic surgery followed by pathology-guided adjuvant oxaliplatin–fluoropyrimidine-based chemotherapy for 3 or 6 months is the current standard approach for patients with stage III and high-risk stage II colon cancer.5, 6, 7 However, up to 20%-30% of patients experience recurrence within 5 years, highlighting the need for novel strategies aimed at improving clinical outcomes.8,9

In the last decade, neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC) has emerged as a potential therapeutic option for patients with LACC patients. Although several concerns exist, such as overtreatment due to radiologic overstaging, the risk of disease progression during preoperative chemotherapy, and a potential increase in surgical complications, NAC has shown several advantages, including the early initiation of systemic therapy, tumor downstaging, improved surgical resectability, better compliance compared with adjuvant chemotherapy (AC), reduced risk of surgical tumor cell dissemination, opportunity for prehabilitation, and in vivo assessment of chemosensitivity.10, 11, 12

Indeed, several clinical trials have been conducted in recent years using various NAC regimens across different clinical settings, which have contributed to the complementarity and robustness of the findings.13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18 Our research group has investigated the impact of NAC in resectable LACC for more than 15 years. Initial efforts have focused on evaluating its safety profile,19 with subsequent analysis assessing tumor response20 and midterm oncologic outcomes.21 This preliminary experience laid the groundwork for this randomized trial.

The ELECLA trial aimed to add to the existing evidence by using a particularly pragmatic approach to investigate the efficacy of a short, standard NAC regimen in patients with proficient mismatch repair (pMMR) LACC.

sec.title: Study design
sec.p: ELECLA is a randomized, multicenter, parallel-group, open-label, phase II controlled clinical trial. The trial design was described in detail previously.22 Recruitment was discontinued early following the recommendation of the independent Data Monitoring Committee, which was composed of four oncologists and one surgeon, and with approval from the Spanish Agency of Medicines and Medical Devices and the Ethics Committee, due to loss of clinical equipoise after emerging evidence supporting neoadjuvant strategies.23 Therefore, the present analysis represents a preplanned interim analysis of the ELECLA trial.

The primary objective of this study was to determine whether NAC, surgery, and AC (intervention group) improve the 2-year disease-free survival (DFS) compared with upfront surgery followed by AC (control group) in patients with LACC patients. The secondary objectives of this study included, in both groups, assessment of the toxicity profile and therapeutic compliance, postoperative morbidity, computed tomography (CT) scan accuracy for LACC diagnosis in the control group and for tumor regression grading (TRG) after NAC in the investigational group. We also aimed to validate the applicability of pathologic TRG—commonly employed in rectal cancer—for colon cancer and to assess whether the NAC regimen improves 2-year DFS and 2- and 5-year overall survival (OS).

sec.title: Eligibility criteria
sec.p: The inclusion criteria included histologically confirmed colon adenocarcinoma, age >18 years, both males and females, good Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status (0-2), adequate hematologic and biochemical parameters, no contraindications to chemotherapy, provision of written and oral informed consent, radiologic diagnosis of resectable T3 tumors with >5 mm extramural invasion or T4 stage on CT scan, any nodal stage, absence of distant metastases, and suitability for elective open or laparoscopic surgery. The exclusion criteria included significant comorbidities, prior malignancy within 5 years, uncontrolled infection, breastfeeding or pregnancy, grade >1 peripheral neuropathy, rectal cancer, bowel obstruction, metastases or carcinomatosis, and microsatellite instability (Supplementary Table S1, available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.108250).

All patients underwent medical history taking, physical examination, colonoscopy with biopsy and microsatellite instability testing, full blood work, and contrast-enhanced CT (1.5 mm slices). Right-sided colon cancer was defined as a tumor located proximal to the splenic flexure, whereas left-sided colon cancer was defined as a tumor extending from the splenic flexure to the sigmoid colon.

Eligible, consenting participants were centrally randomly assigned at a 1:1 ratio to the intervention or control group, stratified by tumor (T) and node (N) stage. Randomization was performed after consent was obtained, ensuring allocation concealment at enrollment.

sec.title: Interventions
sec.p: Patients in the investigational group received three 21-day cycles of CAPOX (capecitabine 1000 mg/m2 days 1-14 + oxaliplatin 130 mg/m2 day 1) or five cycles of biweekly FOLFOX [oxaliplatin 85 mg/m2; leucovorin 400 mg/m2; 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) 400 mg/m2 bolus; continuous infusion of 5-FU 2400 mg/m2 over 46 hours], at the oncologist’s discretion. Surgery was scheduled 4 weeks after NAC, followed by five additional cycles of CAPOX or seven of FOLFOX beginning 4-6 weeks after surgery.
Patients in the control group underwent upfront surgery followed by AC (8 cycles of CAPOX or 12 cycles of FOLFOX) based on the pathologic findings.

sec.title: Outcome parameters
sec.p: DFS was defined as the time from random assignment to the date of occurrence of distant metastases, locoregional recurrence after R0/R1 resection, local R2 resection, unresectable local progression, or death.24 Second primary cancers were not considered events. Patients without relapse were censored at the last follow-up. Distant recurrence was defined as metastases to other organs, distant nodes, or the peritoneum. Locoregional recurrence was defined as relapse at the anastomosis site or surgical field.

OS was defined as the time from randomization to the date of death from any cause or the last follow-up. Radiologic TRG was evaluated 3 weeks after NAC completion by comparing pre- and post-NAC TNM (tumor–node–metastasis) stage and tumor volume according to the RECIST criteria.25 Pathologic TRG was evaluated using a modified Ryan scale.26 The radiologic and pathologic responses were correlated in the investigational group. The accuracy of radiologic staging was assessed in the control group.

Postoperative morbidity was classified using the Clavien–Dindo system, with grades III-V indicating severe complications.27 Chemotherapy toxicity was evaluated using Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 4.0.28

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Categorical variables are presented as counts and percentages, whereas quantitative variables are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD) or median and interquartile range (IQR). Survival analysis was performed in the modified intention-to-treat (mITT) population. The DFS and OS curves were estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method. The equality of survivor functions across groups was evaluated using the log-rank test. Hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for DFS and OS were calculated using multivariate Cox regression models, adjusted for clinically relevant covariates. A P value <0.05 indicated statistical significance. All analyses were performed using Stata 18 (release 18, 2023; StataCorp LLC., College Station, TX).

A total of 238 patients (119 per arm) were required to detect a 15% absolute improvement in 2-year DFS (from 75% to 90%) with 80% power and a two-sided alpha of 0.05, accounting for a 5% dropout rate.

sec.title: Ethical considerations
sec.p: This trial was approved by the local ethics committee (Ref: 1673) and the Spanish Agency of Medicines and Medical Devices. This trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04188158; EudraCT: 2016-002970-10; AEMPS: 16-0553). All adverse events were reported to the sponsor within 24 hours. Annual reviews of cumulative data were conducted by the independent Trial Steering Committee and Data Monitoring Ethics Committee. Annual pharmacovigilance reports were prepared according to the Spanish Clinical Research Network. This study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Recruitment was stopped early after a recommendation from the Data Monitoring Committee due to loss of clinical equipoise. A total of 134 patients were enrolled from 12 hospitals in Spain between March 2017 and June 2024. Of the 134 patients, 14 were excluded, and the remaining 120 were included in the mITT population. Of the 120 patients, 52 were included in the investigational group, and 68 were included in the control group (Figure 1).

Table 1 shows the demographic and tumor characteristics. The mean age of the overall cohort was 63.5 years (SD 10.1), and 64.2% of patients were male (n = 77). Screening was the most common reason for consultation (35.8%), and the sigmoid colon was the most frequent tumor location (29.2%). Furthermore, 26.7% of patients (n = 32) had T4 tumors, and 79.2% (n = 95) showed nodal involvement at baseline CT scan.

sec.title: Investigational group
sec.p: A total of 94.2% of patients (49 of 52) completed all planned NAC cycles, and all patients received at least one neoadjuvant cycle. The median number of CAPOX cycles administered was 3 (IQR 3-3). According to the study protocol, single-agent fluoropyrimidines could be considered for patients older than 70 years or with relevant comorbidities, given the inconclusive evidence regarding the addition of oxaliplatin in this setting. However, in the present cohort, all patients received oxaliplatin-based doublet chemotherapy (CAPOX or FOLFOX), and no patients received fluoropyrimidine-only treatment, at the discretion of the treating physician.

Approximately 94.2% of patients received CAPOX, and 5.8% received FOLFOX. Drug dose reduction was required in 5.8% of patients, and treatment delay was required in 13.5% of patients. The median time from randomization to the first NAC cycle was 10.6 days (IQR 4.2-13.7), and the median time from randomization to surgery was 103 days (IQR 90-111). All patients underwent R0 resection without any unexpected intraoperative findings. Four (7.7%) patients required earlier surgery due to a microperforation (n = 1) or subocclusive episodes (n = 3). One of these patients experienced tumor recurrence during follow-up.

In the NAC group, the radiologic assessment showed a significant reduction in the mean tumor volume from 43.8 cm3 (SD 27.1) to 15.1 cm3 (SD 16.9), corresponding to an overall 65.4% decrease (P < 0.001; Supplementary Figure S1, available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.108250). Additionally, radiologic downstaging was significant in T and N stages (both P < 0.001; Figure 2A and B). No distant progression was observed during NAC. Serum carcinoembryonic antigen decreased from 18.1 to 4.6 ng/mL (P = 0.78).

sec.p: Of the 52 patients, four did not receive AC: three at the oncologist’s discretion, and one due to postoperative death. Nine (18.7%) patients experienced treatment delays during AC, and 12 (25%) required dose modifications. Capecitabine was discontinued in four (8.3%) patients, and oxaliplatin was discontinued in 13 (27.1%), primarily due to neurotoxicity.

sec.title: Control group
sec.p: Preoperative imaging studies overstaged 13 (19.1%) patients who were ultimately diagnosed with low-risk stage II disease on final pathology. According to current clinical practice, assigning these patients to the investigational group would likely result in overtreatment. The median time from randomization to surgery was 38.7 days (IQR 20-46).

Intraoperative findings revealed one case of an unresectable tumor, one case of liver metastasis, and one case of peritoneal carcinomatosis, all of which were undetected by baseline CT scan. Of the 68 patients, one (1.5%) required emergency surgery due to abdominal pain and fever, and this patient subsequently relapsed.

Among the 68 patients in the control group, 13 had low-risk stage II disease on final pathology and therefore did not meet the criteria for AC according to current guidelines. Of the remaining 55 patients who were candidates for adjuvant treatment, one died in the immediate postoperative period and two were not fit enough to receive adjuvant therapy due to poor postoperative condition. Furthermore, three were found to have metastatic disease (two diagnosed intraoperatively and one with liver metastases on the first postoperative CT scan). The remaining patient had an unresectable tumor at surgery. Consequently, 48 patients received AC according to the planned protocol (47 CAPOX and one FOLFOX). Treatment delays occurred in 20 patients (41.6%) and dose modifications in 18 patients (37.5%). Capecitabine was discontinued in six patients (12.5%), and oxaliplatin in 16 patients (33.3%).

sec.title: Postoperative outcomes
sec.p: The control group underwent a higher proportion of laparoscopic procedures than the intervention group (91.2% versus 80.7%; P = 0.097). The intervention group exhibited numerically lower rates of anastomotic leakage (1.9% versus 9.0%; P = 0.13) and severe complications (5.8% versus 13.2%; P = 0.18). No significant difference in hospital stay was observed between the two groups (5.9 versus 6.7 days; P = 0.42; Supplementary Table S2, available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.108250).

sec.title: Pathologic findings
sec.p: NAC was associated with a higher degree of downstaging of both primary tumor and regional lymph nodes compared with upfront surgery: pT0-1-2 (23.1% versus 8.8%, P = 0.03) and N0 (59.6% versus 40.4%, P = 0.008). Pathologic early-stage disease was more frequent in the intervention group (P = 0.026; Figure 3).

sec.p: In the surgical specimen, patients who received NAC achieved a significantly lower rate of poor prognostic features, such as lymphatic invasion (P = 0.009), tumor budding (P = 0.002), vascular invasion (P = 0.077), and positive lymph node count (P = 0.06). No differences were observed in the incidence of perineural invasion (P = 0.938) between groups. Incomplete resections (unresectable tumors, R1/R2, or residual metastases) were less frequently reported in the investigational group (0% versus 7.4%; P = 0.068). Among the 43 patients of the NAC group with a reported pathologic TRG, 51.2% achieved TRG 0-2 (Table 2).

sec.title: Survival outcomes
sec.p: At the time of this interim analysis, not all patients had completed 24 months of follow-up. After a median follow-up of 37.2 months (IQR 16.0-62.3), five (9.6%) recurrences occurred in the intervention group compared with 12 (17.6%) in the control group (HR 0.49, 95% CI 0.17-1.41, P = 0.18). The 2-year DFS rate was 88.9% (95% CI 75.2% to 95.2%) in the intervention group and 83.3% (95% CI 70.9% to 90.7%) in the control group (P = 0.34; Figure 4A). The number of deaths was numerically lower in the investigational group (n = 2) than in the control group (n = 7; HR 0.36, 95% CI 0.07-1.73, P = 0.20). The 2-year OS rate was 98.1% (95% CI 87.1% to 99.7%) in the intervention group and 93.4% (95% CI 83.3% to 97.5%) in the control group (P = 0.28; Figure 4B).

sec.p: The subgroup analysis of DFS revealed no significant interactions between baseline characteristics and treatment group. Although not statistically significant, patients aged ≤65 years and those with cT4 tumors or cN+ disease appeared to derive the greatest benefit from NAC in terms of DFS (Supplementary Figure S2, available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.108250).

In both groups, no recurrences were observed in patients with a favorable prognosis (pathologic stages 0-II without high-risk features; P = 0.007; Supplementary Figure S3, available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.108250), whereas patients with a pathologic high-risk stage II, III, or IV had a significantly increased risk of recurrence (HR 7.27, P = 0.008; Supplementary Figure S4, available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.108250). Patients in the NAC group had a higher likelihood of achieving pathologic favorable features (44.2% versus 19.1%; P = 0.003).

Patients in the investigational group who achieved a good pathologic TRG (Ryan TRG 0-2) had improved DFS compared with those with a poor response (Supplementary Figure S5, available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.108250). Although a good pathologic TRG was more frequent in women (61.5% versus 38.4%) and in patients with left-sided tumors (56% versus 44.4%), these differences did not reach statistical significance (P = 0.37 and P = 0.45, respectively). A favorable radiologic response was associated with a better pathologic response (P = 0.076). Notably, 75% of patients with radiologic response demonstrated pathologic response (Supplementary Figure S6, available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.108250).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The results of this randomized trial support the feasibility and tolerability of NAC in patients with resectable pMMR LACC, as reflected by the absence of increased perioperative morbidity and high treatment compliance. Importantly, this interim analysis did not demonstrate statistical superiority in 2-year DFS. Therefore, survival outcomes should be interpreted cautiously and considered exploratory, particularly given the limited statistical power resulting from early trial termination.

The role of NAC in LACC still remains controversial,4 with current guidelines recommending NAC only conditionally, primarily for more advanced stages.5,29,30 Nevertheless, several recent randomized trials and meta-analyses have suggested that NAC is a safe and feasible treatment option, with promising efficacy outcomes in terms of relapse risk reduction and long-term survival times.13, 14, 15, 16,31, 32, 33, 34 The results of the ELECLA trial are consistent with this growing body of evidence.35,36

Current knowledge suggests that NAC protocols should consider MMR status and exclude dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase deficiency, both of which are eligibility criteria in the ELECLA trial.22 Deficient mismatch repair (dMMR) tumors account for 13.5%-18.2% of LACC cases and have limited response to NAC, as confirmed in the OPTICAL and FOxTROT trials.13,15,16 Given the remarkable tumor responses achieved with neoadjuvant immunotherapy in dMMR rectal cancer and the remarkable findings of the NICHE-1 trial, evaluating its impact in dMMR LACC is ongoing.37,38

Several studies have shown that adding monoclonal antibodies to NAC regimens only benefits a subset of molecularly selected patients with LACC patients, and its use remains investigational.36,39, 40, 41 In this sense, a pragmatic oxaliplatin–fluoropyrimidine regimen, aligned with standard clinical practice, was selected in the ELECLA trial. The FOxTROT-3 trial is currently evaluating the potential benefit of adding irinotecan to a neoadjuvant triplet regimen, exploring preoperative intensification in fit patients.42 In addition, the UNICORN trial is assessing the role of preoperative targeted therapy based on individual molecular profile added to surgery and standard AC.43

In the ELECLA trial, 7.7% of patients required early surgery due to NAC-related complications. However, all of these patients achieved R0 resection without postoperative morbidity. In the FOxTROT trial, 4.3% of patients developed obstruction during NAC.13 In our cohort, 75% of subocclusive events occurred in T4 tumors, consistent with previous findings.

NAC provides a window of opportunity for patient prehabilitation, anemia correction, nutrition optimization, and fitness improvement, which may contribute to similar or even reduced rates of surgical complications.13,23,34,44,45 In the FOxTROT trial, NAC was associated with a lower risk of anastomotic leakage and a lower rate of complications requiring reoperation (4.7% versus 7.4%, P = 0.07; 4.3% versus 7.1%, P = 0.05, respectively).13 These findings are consistent with those of the ELECLA trial.

The risk of overtreatment due to radiologic overstaging remains a challenge.46, 47, 48 In the FOxTROT and PRODIGE22 trials, 24% and 33% of patients who were initially staged as LACC were finally found to have a pathologic low-risk stage II disease and therefore would not typically meet the criteria for AC.13,34 In the ELECLA trial, overstaging occurred in 19.1% of patients in the control group. Therefore, improved imaging techniques, such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or positron emission tomography (PET)/CT, are being actively explored.49 Alternatively, emerging concepts, such as tumor deposits and extramural venous invasion on CT, may improve patient selection.50,51 An important challenge lies in the accurate identification of patients at higher baseline risk who are most likely to benefit from neoadjuvant strategies. In our cohort, exploratory analyses suggested that patients with cT4 tumors, nodal involvement, or age ≤65 years may derive greater benefit (Supplementary Figure S2, available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.108250). The correlation observed between radiologic and pathologic responses in the ELECLA trial further supports the potential value of imaging-based response assessment during neoadjuvant treatment. If validated in larger cohorts, radiologic response could represent a useful early marker of treatment sensitivity and may help guide treatment strategies in future studies.

In the present trial, the NAC completion rate reached 94.2%, which is consistent with other studies,13,15 and remains a major advantage of this approach. The investigational group exhibited better treatment compliance, which may be partly explained by the avoidance of postoperative complications that can delay or limit the administration of AC. In contrast, AC completion rates remain suboptimal, even with the newer short-course regimens.52 Importantly, delays in AC have been reported to be associated with worse survival, with each 4-week delay being associated with a 14% decrease in OS.53

The findings of the ELECLA trial provide valuable insight into treatment response. The radiologic and carcinoembryonic antigen responses were favorable, making it one of the few studies to systematically assess treatment response from this perspective. Additionally, this trial reported a favorable pathologic response rate (TRG 0-2) of 51.2%, which is within the range reported by other trials (44%-63%).15,34 Given the limited number of events and sample size, perineural invasion (P = 0.043) and poor Ryan response (P = 0.048) were the only significant pathologic predictors of recurrence among patients treated with NAC (Supplementary Material, available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.108250). This finding is consistent with previous studies from our group, underscoring the prognostic importance of perineural invasion in both rectal and colon cancer.54,55 However, this finding warrants further investigation.

In this trial, NAC an achieved a R0 resection rate of 100%, which is consistent with the FOxTROT trial (94%). Pathologic downstaging and reduced prevalence of adverse pathologic features may all have contributed to improved outcomes and are consistent with those of the FOxTROT and OPTICAL trials.13,15 In the FOxTROT trial, patients who achieved complete regression after NAC experienced a 0% recurrence rate compared with 29% among those without regression. These findings are consistent with those of our study and further validate the prognostic impact of pathologic TRG in LACC. In this line, one may speculate whether a longer course of NAC may further improve response, particularly in patients with low obstructive risk.17,56

The strength of the ELECLA trial lies in its real-world design, which has no upper age limit and addresses the common underrepresentation of older patients in trials.5 In contrast to the OPTICAL trial, which observed improved DFS in women (HR 0.54, 95% CI 0.30-0.95), the ELECLA trial did not find significant sex-based differences.15

The present results should be interpreted as an interim analysis of an underpowered trial. The trial was originally powered to detect a 15% absolute improvement in 2-year DFS. However, early termination of recruitment resulted in a smaller sample size than initially planned, limiting the statistical power to detect differences in long-term survival outcomes. Notably, early trial termination entails the risk of overestimation bias, nonproportional hazards, and recruitment heterogeneity.57 Therefore, survival results should be interpreted as exploratory and hypothesis-generating. Further limitations include the relatively small sample size and short follow-up period. However, we are committed to reporting the long-term 5-year endpoints. Despite these limitations, the survival trends observed in the ELECLA trial are numerically consistent with those reported in larger randomized trials such as FOxTROT and OPTICAL.13,15

The ELECLA trial contributes to the growing body of evidence supporting the use of NAC in pMMR LACC. The findings of this trial are consistent with ongoing evaluations of more radical surgical approaches, such as complete mesocolic excision with central vascular ligation or D3 lymphadenectomy, aimed at improving patient outcomes.58 All this background underscores the need to manage LACC within dedicated multidisciplinary tumor boards.30,31

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: NAC demonstrated a favorable safety and feasibility profile in patients with resectable pMMR LACC. Although no significant survival advantage was observed in this interim analysis, NAC was associated with improved tumor downstaging and favorable pathologic features. These findings support the feasibility of this strategy and warrant further investigation in larger studies, which should also focus on refining patient selection.
